title.value: EvilHarmony: Stealthy Adversarial Attacks against Black-box Speech Recognition Systems
EvilHarmony: Stealthy Adversarial Attacks against Black-box Speech Recognition Systems

abstract.value: Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) systems are vulnerable to adversarial examples (AEs), where small, carefully designed perturbations are added to original audio to mislead the systems into generating target commands. Existing adversarial attacks typically initialize perturbations either as zero or as Text-to-Speech clips of the target command. The former accumulates the features of the command in the perturbed audio, while the latter constantly reduces the features of the command, resulting in the generation of AEs. Although most target commands in the AEs are imperceptible to humans, the audio often exhibits noticeable distortions or disruptions, making it apparent that the sound has been tampered with. This work aims to retain only the essential features of adversarial audio, minimizing distortions from unnecessary elements to improve quality and make the attack less detectable. Our findings highlight the importance of formants as critical features for black-box adversarial attacks, motivating the development of a novel Formant Filter Bank (FFB) tailored to the target command. By inputting musical audio into the FFB, we utilize the filtered output as the perturbation seed, which retains the formant features of the target command and blends in certain features of the original music. Then we search for a minimum enhancement factor for the perturbation seed to generate high-quality AEs. Our perturbation can be regarded as local amplitude modulation of the music, so we define the AE as EvilHarmony. Experimental results demonstrate that our method successfully attacks commercial black-box ASR models, including Microsoft, Google, Amazon, Tencentyun, Aliyun, and OpenAI Whisper-V3. Compared to existing approaches, our AEs achieve significantly greater stealth, with 53% to 77% of participants perceiving them as indistinguishable from normal audio across the six ASR API services. Additionally, our approach successfully attacks Google Assistant and voice assistants on Surface Pro 9 in the real world. Demos are uploaded at https://sites.google.com/view/evilharmony.

Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) systems are vulnerable to adversarial examples (AEs), where small, carefully designed perturbations are added to original audio to mislead the systems into generating target commands. Existing adver- sarial attacks typically initialize perturbations either as zero or as Text-to-Speech clips of the target command. The former accumulates the features of the command in the perturbed audio, while the latter constantly reduces the features of the command, resulting in the generation of AEs. Although most target commands in the AEs are imperceptible to humans, the audio often exhibits noticeable distortions or disruptions, making it apparent that the sound has been tampered with. This work aims to retain only the essential features of adversarial audio, minimizing distortions from unnecessary elements to improve quality and make the attack less detectable. Then we search for a minimum enhancement factor for the perturbation seed to generate high-quality AEs. Our perturbation can be regarded as local amplitude modulation of the music, so we define the AE as EvilHarmony. Additionally, our approach successfully attacks Google Assistant and voice assistants on Surface Pro 9 in the real world. Demos are uploaded at https://sites.google.com/view/evilharmony . ∗Corresponding author: chenkai@iie.ac.cn. 1. Introduction Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) technology has become widely used in various applications, including virtual assistants, customer service chat-bots, and transcription services. However, ASR systems remain vulnerable to var- ious attacks. For instance, DolphinAttack [ 60] and Light Commands [ 47] leverage inaudible carriers, e.g., ultrasonic or laser, to transmit target commands like “open the camera”. Hidden voice command [ 15, 20, 49] distort human speech into noises, rendering the semantic content indiscernible to humans. However, inaudible attacks require special signal transmitters, which are not commonly available in daily life. Hidden voice commands are often too noisy, making them easily capture human attention. Therefore, they are hard to widely spread. We aim to research AEs with good sound quality that are easily spread and accepted by human beings. Adversarial examples (AEs) [ 21, 23, 24, 25, 26, 28, 38, 42, 45, 46, 51, 52, 53, 56, 57, 63] are generated by carefully adding small perturbation into common audio (e.g., music) to mislead ASR models into outputting target commands, which are imperceptible to humans. In white-box adversarial attacks, researchers can design a special objective function [ 21, 46, 52, 56, 57, 63] based on the principles of ASR algorithms, the model parameters, or its output. Given an original audio clip and a target command, they search for small perturbations that optimize the objective function [ 21, 23, 24, 25, 28, 42, 45, 46, 53, 57, 63]. If the perturbed audio causes the objective function to converge, it becomes a potential AE for the ASR model. In black-box settings, adversarial attacks primarily rely on transferable AEs of white-box models [ 24] or by continuously querying the target ASR model to generate AEs [ 28, 63]. A notable example of feature-based attacks involves Mel- frequency Cepstral Coefficients (MFCC), widely used in speech recognition. Researchers have demonstrated adver- sarial attacks by manipulating MFCC features of AEs to mimic those of Text-to-Speech (TTS) audio corresponding 4569 DOI 10.1109/SP61157.2025.00259 to the target command [ 20, 52]. However, MFCC inherently contains redundant features that, when removed, can improve the stealthiness of AEs ( Section 4 ). To define “stealthiness”, most existing works consider an AE stealthy if its target commands are inaudible to humans, even if the audio quality is poor. In this work, we propose a more practical definition of stealthiness: an AE is stealthy if its target commands are imperceptible to human listeners while maintaining acceptable sound quality, free from noticeable distortions or disruptions. Specifically, we address two research questions: (Q1) What are the critical features in the AEs that make the black- box adversarial attack successful? (Q2) How can we generate highly stealthy AEs incorporating these critical features to attack popular commercial black-box ASR models? The generated AEs should be uninterpretable and surreptitious to the victim users without easily alerting them during the attack. Key Findings. We analyzed AEs generated by existing black- box adversarial attacks [ 24, 25, 52, 63], and found that their first-order, second-order, and third-order formant tracks are similar to those of the target commands. Our probing tests demonstrate that audio clips containing these formants can effectively deceive multiple ASR models. Thus, we conclude that those formants are critical features for successful black- box adversarial attacks (addressing Q1). Moreover, previous research suggests that using lp-norm, band-pass filters, and psychological masking effects can limit perturbations to the original audio (i.e., the carrier), making the target commands in the AEs uninterpretable to humans [ 21, 42, 45, 46, 53, 57]. Our study takes this a step further by constructing the critical formant features of the target command from the carrier's features, such as borrowing partial features of the carrier to form the critical formant features of the target command, resulting in even more surreptitious AEs (addressing Q2) . Our Solution . Based on our findings, we developed Evil- Harmony, a formant-guided adversarial attack. The process is as follows: We extract the formants from each frame of TTS audio of the target command, obtaining a formant center matrix. Using each element of the formant center matrix as the frequency of a filter, we construct a formant filter bank (FFB). This setup ensures that the frequencies near the target command's formants fall within the pass- bands of the FFB, preserving the formant features of the target command in the filtered audio. The original audio is then input into the FFB, and the resulting filtered audio is used as a perturbation seed. We identify the minimum multiplier needed to amplify the perturbation seed, enabling the perturbed audio to be recognized as the target command by the ASR model. As the perturbation seeds incorporate features from both the original audio and the target command, the generated AEs are both stealthy and robust. Since existing robust attacks are typically limited to near- field ranges of 5 ∼15cm between the speaker and intelligent voice control (IVC) devices [ 24, 52], we designed our physical-world attack using ten target commands related to everyday expressions, with speaker-to-ASR system distances ranging from 5 cm to 15 cm. Experimental results show that EvilHarmony achieves a 100% success rate in generating AEs to attack multiple black-box ASR API services, in- cluding Microsoft, Google, Amazon, Aliyun, Tencentyun, and OpenAI Whisper. Across these six services, 53% to 77% of participants perceive our AEs as indistinguishable from normal audio, demonstrating the stealthiness of our attack. Additionally, our approach generates transferable AEs that can successfully attack various voice assistants, such as Google Assistant on Google Pixel 4 and the voice assistant on Surface Pro 9 in the real world; 51% of participants perceive these physical-world AEs as indistinguishable from legitimate commands. Furthermore, our AEs are capable of attacking the voice input systems of large language models, including Doubao of ByteDance [ 4]. Contribution. The contributions of this paper are as follows. • New findings. Our investigation reveals that the formants of the target command are critical features in AEs for misleading black-box ASR models. Thus, directly obtaining perturba- tions that preserve the target command's formant features, rather than “blindly” searching for noisy perturbations across the entire feature space , can generate high-quality AEs for general black-box ASR models. • New technique. We propose Formant Filter Banks (FFB), which extract perturbation seeds containing the formant features of the target command along with segments of the original audio. Using these seeds, we optimize the minimum amplification factor needed to generate AEs. Our method, EvilHarmony, surpasses existing approaches by better concealing the target command while preserving good audio quality. 2. Background 2.1.
